c-neuro-05-q045.hinge: Severe carbon monoxide poisoning presenting with loss of consciousness and normal PaO2 mandates hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
c-neuro-05-q045.trap: Coma in an unknown unresponsive patient tempts empiric naloxone, but trailer heating exposure and pink mucosa confirm CO poisoning.

A.clue: Displaces carboxyhemoglobin and prevents sequelae
A.fit: Here: coma, trailer resident, pink mucosa, normal PaO2

B.clue: Reduces methemoglobin back to ferrous hemoglobin
B.fit: Not here: cyanosis absent; treats methemoglobinemia, not CO

C.fit: Not here: pupils 4 mm, normal respirations 20/min, no drug history

D.fit: Not here: not an anticholinergic toxidrome; risk of cholinergic toxicity

nodes.text: Unresponsive patient from enclosed space + normal PaO2: measure carboxyhemoglobin via co-oximetry
Immediately apply 100% normobaric oxygen via tight non-rebreather mask
Indications for hyperbaric oxygen: loss of consciousness, carboxyhemoglobin > 25%, ischemic ECG changes, pregnancy
**Severe metabolic lactic acidosis or cardiac ischemia:** transfer immediately to hyperbaric chamber
**Mild symptoms without loss of consciousness or pregnancy:** continue normobaric oxygen until asymptomatic
Obtain serial ECG and troponin to screen for myocardial injury
Follow-up neuropsychological evaluation for delayed neurological sequelae (Parkinsonism, memory loss)

c-neuro-05-q046.hinge: A patient with locked-in syndrome possessing decision-making capacity has the autonomous right to decline life support, regardless of family disagreement.
c-neuro-05-q046.trap: Threat of litigation by an estranged daughter tempts seeking a court order, but a capable patient's autonomous decision is paramount.

A.clue: Judicial intervention when surrogate disputes occur
A.fit: Not here: patient has capacity, superseding family disputes and courts
A.tempting: estranged daughter does not and is threatening legal action

B.clue: Ethics consultation serving an advisory role
B.fit: Not here: competent patient makes final decision, not ethics committee

C.clue: Surrogate consensus required only when incapacitated
C.fit: Not here: competent patient decision overrides all surrogate opinions

D.clue: Artificial hydration continuation against patient wishes
D.fit: Not here: patient explicitly refused artificial hydration as well

E.clue: Autonomous patient right to refuse interventions
E.fit: Here: locked-in patient with capacity requests withdrawal of life support

algorithm.title: End-of-life decision making in locked-in syndrome

nodes.text: Locked-in syndrome from pontine stroke: patient retains full consciousness and cognitive capacity
Establish reliable communication code (eye blinks or vertical gaze) to assess decision-making capacity
Patient demonstrates capacity: autonomous refusal of life support (ventilator and hydration) must be honored
**Family member objects or threatens litigation:** counsel family that competent patient autonomy legally supersedes surrogate wishes
Transition goal of care to comprehensive palliative comfort measures and symptom control
Administer intravenous opioids (morphine) and benzodiazepines to relieve air hunger and distress
Perform compassionate terminal extubation in peaceful setting with family present

c-neuro-05-q047.trap: Lateral thigh sensory changes tempt lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (meralgia paresthetica), but motor weakness and reflex loss confirm femoral neuropathy.

nodes.text: Acute severe thigh pain + proximal quadriceps weakness + loss of patellar reflex: femoral neuropathy
Recognize diabetic etiology (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy or isolated femoral mononeuropathy)
Perform electromyography and nerve conduction studies: active denervation in femoral-innervated muscles
Perform retroperitoneal and pelvic imaging (CT or MRI) to exclude compressive hematoma or mass
**Compressive retroperitoneal hematoma:** surgical or interventional evacuation
**Diabetic amyotrophy (microvascular ischemia):** optimize glycemic control + consider short-course immunotherapy
Physical therapy with knee bracing to prevent falls + neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy

c-neuro-05-q048.hinge: Infantile regression with spasticity, irritability, optic atrophy, and consanguinity defines Krabbe leukodystrophy, characterized by diffuse white matter degeneration.
c-neuro-05-q048.trap: Intermittent low-grade fever tempts congenital infection with periventricular calcifications, but developmental regression with spasticity signifies leukodystrophy.

A.clue: Cerebellar vermis underdevelopment with ataxia
A.fit: Not here: extensive cerebral white matter demyelination in Krabbe

B.clue: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causing diffuse demyelination
B.fit: Here: developmental regression, optic atrophy, spasticity, consanguineous parents

C.clue: Failure of forebrain cleavage into hemispheres
C.fit: Not here: post-developmental regression after normal early infancy

D.clue: Ventricular dilatation from impaired CSF dynamics
D.fit: Not here: primary leukodystrophic white matter destruction

E.clue: Intracranial calcifications from congenital TORCH infection
E.fit: Not here: neurodegenerative leukodystrophy without calcifications

F.fit: Not here: normal initial development followed by rapid regression

G.fit: Not here: extensive leukodystrophy with marked white matter destruction

nodes.text: Infantile developmental regression + irritability + spasticity + optic atrophy: suspect Krabbe leukodystrophy
Perform brain MRI: extensive bilateral white matter demyelination and degeneration
Confirm diagnosis: measure galactocerebrosidase enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
Identify pathognomonic multinucleated globoid cells on histology or genetic GALC testing
**Pre-symptomatic or newborn screening diagnosis:** early hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
**Symptomatic infantile onset:** comprehensive multidisciplinary supportive and palliative care
Manage spasticity and seizures with baclofen and antiseizure medications

c-neuro-05-q049.hinge: Distal sensory polyneuropathy in AIDS is treated first-line with neuropathic pain agents, specifically tricyclic antidepressants like nortriptyline.
c-neuro-05-q049.trap: Burning pain in the feet tempts localized topical lidocaine, but diffuse bilateral hands and feet involvement requires systemic neuromodulation.

B.fit: Not here: does not treat neuropathic pain pathways

C.fit: Here: AIDS, painful burning in hands and feet

D.fit: Not here: worsens opportunistic infection risk in AIDS

E.fit: Not here: generalized bilateral stocking-glove neuropathic pain

nodes.text: HIV/AIDS patient with distal burning paresthesias and allodynia: diagnose HIV sensory polyneuropathy
Screen for contributing causes: neurotoxic antiretrovirals (didanosine, stavudine), B12 deficiency, diabetes
Initiate first-line systemic neuropathic pharmacotherapy: oral nortriptyline or gabapentin
**Intolerant or unresponsive to tricyclics:** switch to pregabalin or duloxetine
**Severe refractory burning pain:** add low-dose topical capsaicin or short-term tramadol
Optimize antiretroviral therapy (suppressive ART without neurotoxic reverse transcriptase inhibitors)
Foot care education and routine neurological surveillance to prevent trophic ulcers

c-neuro-05-q050.boardCall: Prolonged IV gentamicin therapy + bilateral hearing loss + tinnitus + oscillopsia/ataxia -> Aminoglycoside ototoxicity
c-neuro-05-q050.hinge: Bilateral sensorineural deafness with vestibular ataxia following prolonged parenteral gentamicin defines aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity and ototoxicity.
c-neuro-05-q050.trap: Episodic vertigo and tinnitus mimic Meniere disease, but recent prolonged gentamicin therapy and bilateral sensorineural loss establish ototoxicity.

A.clue: Gentamicin destruction of cochlear hair cells
A.fit: Here: bilateral deafness, vestibular ataxia following prolonged IV gentamicin

B.clue: Vestibular schwannoma causing unilateral hearing loss
B.fit: Not here: bilateral hearing loss directly following IV gentamicin

C.clue: Endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo
C.fit: Not here: severe bilateral permanent loss following aminoglycosides

D.clue: Brainstem ischemic stroke with cranial palsies
D.fit: Not here: pure audiovestibular syndrome without motor or sensory deficits

E.clue: Postviral vertigo with intact hearing
E.fit: Not here: severe bilateral hearing loss and bilateral nystagmus

nodes.text: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss + oscillopsia + ataxia after gentamicin: aminoglycoside toxicity
Recognize mechanism: aminoglycosides accumulate in endolymph, destroying cochlear and vestibular hair cells
Perform formal audiometry: high-frequency bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Vestibular testing (caloric testing, video head impulse test): bilateral vestibular hypofunction
Discontinue aminoglycoside immediately if still active; damage is largely irreversible
**Severe disabling bilateral hearing impairment:** evaluate for bilateral cochlear implantation
Vestibular rehabilitation physical therapy to train visual and proprioceptive compensatory balance mechanisms

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, or recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; papillary rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

table.title: Syndrome branches
rows: Urgent catheterization if unstable; otherwise risk-guided angiography
Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common

amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis.scope: Upper and lower motor neuron signs, bulbar symptoms, preserved sensation, EMG/NCS findings, noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, riluzole, edaravone, end-of-life planning
amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis.core: Progressive weakness with upper and lower motor neuron signs in multiple regions, usually with preserved sensation and sphincter function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Middle/older adulthood, male sex; mostly sporadic, minority familial
Family history of motor neuron disease or frontotemporal dementia supports inherited susceptibility

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Atrophy, fasciculations + hyperreflexia/spasticity** within affected regions; asymmetric limb onset common
Bulbar disease: dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue wasting; pseudobulbar affect may accompany corticobulbar dysfunction
Orthopnea, morning headache, weak cough, daytime somnolence suggest ventilatory muscle weakness
Ocular movement and sensation usually spared; some patients develop executive or behavioral impairment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Degeneration of corticospinal neurons and anterior horn/bulbar motor neurons; denervation spreads progressively

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical progression + EMG/NCS**: widespread active/chronic denervation; sensory conduction usually normal
MRI brain/spine to exclude structural mimics; targeted B12, thyroid, CK, and other studies
Assess FVC, inspiratory strength, nocturnal gas exchange, swallow function, nutrition; no single definitive blood test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Riluzole** modestly prolongs survival; edaravone may slow functional decline in selected patients
★ **Noninvasive ventilation** for symptomatic respiratory weakness improves comfort and survival
Swallow/nutrition support; discuss gastrostomy before severe respiratory decline; cough-assist and secretion management
Baclofen for spasticity, communication devices, physical/occupational support; multidisciplinary specialty care
Early shared planning for ventilation, feeding, advance directives, hospice; discuss choices before communication declines

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure is usual terminal event; aspiration, malnutrition, falls, immobility
Depression, caregiver burden; frontotemporal impairment may affect decision-making capacity

rows.label: Prevention
items: No primary prevention; aspiration/fall precautions, vaccination, nutritional support, respiratory surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical myelopathy: sensory level, sphincter changes, compressive MRI lesion
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular weakness, no UMN signs
Multifocal motor neuropathy: conduction block, IVIG response

amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis.evidence: Not checked online; established ALS diagnosis and supportive-treatment teaching.

bone-tumors.name: Bone tumors
bone-tumors.scope: Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, giant cell tumor of bone, osteochondroma, osteoid osteoma, bone metastases, biopsy
bone-tumors.core: Persistent focal bone pain, a growing mass, or a destructive radiographic lesion requires planned evaluation before biopsy or fixation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Osteosarcoma: adolescence, prior radiation, Paget disease; chondrosarcoma: older adults
Hereditary multiple exostoses predispose to osteochondromas; most adult malignant bone lesions are metastases

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Night/rest pain**, enlarging mass, constitutional symptoms or pathologic fracture → concerning lesion
Osteoid osteoma: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; small cortical nidus
Osteochondroma: painless metaphyseal exostosis with medullary continuity; new growth after maturity concerning

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor lineage determines osteoid, cartilage or primitive-cell production; aggressive growth destroys cortex
Giant cell tumor: neoplastic stromal cells recruit osteoclast-like giant cells, causing locally aggressive osteolysis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plain radiographs first**; assess location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix
Aggressive lesion → MRI entire involved bone/adjacent joint; chest CT for lung metastases
★ **Orthopedic oncology plans biopsy tract**; core biopsy after imaging, before definitive treatment
CBC, ESR/CRP if infection suspected; normal labs do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Osteosarcoma → **neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide resection**, then postoperative chemotherapy
Ewing → systemic chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation
Chondrosarcoma → wide surgical excision; conventional tumors relatively chemo/radioresistant
Symptomatic osteoid osteoma → radiofrequency ablation; asymptomatic osteochondroma → observation
Giant cell tumor → curettage/reconstruction; selected unresectable lesions → denosumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Pathologic fracture, neurovascular compromise, pulmonary metastases; limb surgery and chemotherapy morbidity

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: infection markers, cultures; may closely resemble Ewing
Bone metastases: older adult, multiple lesions; myeloma: anemia, monoclonal protein

bone-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

brachial-plexus-disorders.name: Brachial plexus disorders
brachial-plexus-disorders.scope: Erb palsy (upper trunk C5-C6), Klumpke palsy (lower trunk C8-T1), thoracic outlet syndrome, radiation-induced brachial plexopathy, neoplastic infiltration (Pancoast tumor), neuralgic amyotrophy
brachial-plexus-disorders.core: Weakness and sensory loss spanning several peripheral nerves in one arm suggest a plexus lesion rather than isolated mononeuropathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Shoulder dystocia, traction injuries, motorcycle crashes; prior breast/axillary radiation
Apical lung tumor, cervical rib, repetitive overhead activity; neuralgic amyotrophy often postinfectious

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Severe shoulder pain followed by weakness** days later → neuralgic amyotrophy
Thoracic outlet: positional lower-plexus symptoms; swelling/cyanosis suggests venous compression
★ Progressive painful lower-trunk deficit plus **Horner syndrome** → Pancoast tumor

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plexus traction, compression, inflammatory injury, or tumor infiltration disrupts multiple terminal nerves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EMG/nerve conduction studies** localize affected trunks; sensory responses reduced, paraspinals usually spared
MRI brachial plexus for structural lesion; chest imaging for lower-trunk symptoms or cancer concern
Vascular thoracic outlet symptoms → duplex ultrasound, CT/MR angiography; provocative maneuvers alone insufficient
★ New deficit after radiation → **exclude recurrent cancer** before attributing to radiation injury

rows.label: Tx
items: Birth traction palsy: range-of-motion rehabilitation; persistent severe deficits → specialist nerve-repair evaluation
Neuralgic amyotrophy: analgesia, physical/occupational therapy; consider early corticosteroids for pain
Neurogenic thoracic outlet: posture modification and physical therapy; refractory objective deficits → decompression
Vascular compromise/thrombosis → urgent vascular evaluation; neoplastic plexopathy → treat malignancy

rows.label: Complications
items: Denervation atrophy, contractures, chronic neuropathic pain; venous thrombosis or distal arterial ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged traction and compressive positioning; maintain shoulder mobility during recovery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck provocation, preserved sensory responses, paraspinal denervation
Rotator cuff tear: mechanical shoulder weakness without distal sensory loss

table.title: Patterns
rows: Adducted, internally rotated arm; extended elbow

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal lesions → personality change; motor cortex → weakness; posterior fossa → ataxia
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Vestibular symptoms → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
Cherry-red skin uncommon; ordinary skin color offers no reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.name: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.scope: Central line infection, organisms, line removal, prevention
catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.core: Fever or rigors in a patient with an intravascular catheter, especially during infusion, raises concern for catheter-related bacteremia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long catheter dwell time, femoral placement, parenteral nutrition, immunosuppression, hemodialysis
Poor asepsis, frequent hub manipulation; tunneled devices and ports also susceptible

rows.label: Clues
items: Exit-site erythema or drainage may occur; normal insertion-site appearance does not exclude infection
★ **Hypotension, persistent bacteremia**, new murmur, or embolic signs → complicated infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Skin flora migrate externally or contaminated hubs seed intraluminal biofilm
Biofilm limits antibiotic penetration; S aureus and Candida frequently seed distant sites

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Before antibiotics: **paired peripheral and catheter blood cultures**, labelled by source
Same organism with catheter culture positive ≥2 h earlier supports catheter source
Culture removed catheter tip when infection suspected; no routine tip culture after elective removal
Repeat blood cultures to document clearance; persistent positivity → endocarditis, infected thrombus, abscess evaluation
S aureus bacteremia → echocardiography, TEE when high risk; assess metastatic foci

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis → **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, adjusted to cultures and local resistance
★ **Remove line** for shock, tunnel infection, endocarditis, persistent bacteremia, S aureus, Pseudomonas, or fungi
Candida → echinocandin; MSSA → cefazolin or nafcillin; enterococcal treatment follows susceptibilities
Selected stable long-term line infections with coagulase-negative staphylococci → systemic antibiotics + antibiotic lock
Uncomplicated S aureus bacteremia: ≥14 days after clearance; endocarditis/deep infection usually requires 4–6 weeks

rows.label: Complications
items: Endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, osteomyelitis, septic emboli, shock
Unnecessary device retention → relapse; repeated placement → thrombosis and vascular injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin preparation, maximal sterile barrier** during insertion
Scrub hubs, sterile dressings, daily necessity review, prompt removal of unnecessary lines
Avoid routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics or scheduled catheter replacement solely to prevent infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contaminated blood culture: single skin-flora isolate without corroborating cultures or illness
Infusate reaction: temporal symptoms without reproducible bacteremia
Catheter thrombosis: swelling, poor flow; cultures negative unless infected

table.title: Organism pattern
rows: Parenteral nutrition, broad antibiotics; remove catheter

catheter-related-bloodstream-infection.evidence: Not checked online; established catheter-infection management principles.

cervical-artery-dissection.name: Cervical artery dissection
cervical-artery-dissection.scope: Carotid artery dissection, vertebral artery dissection, Horner syndrome, posterior circulation stroke, imaging, antithrombotic therapy
cervical-artery-dissection.core: Young or middle-aged adult with sudden unilateral head or neck pain followed by retinal or cerebral ischemia after minor neck trauma.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neck manipulation, hyperextension, sporting injury, coughing; spontaneous cases common
Fibromuscular dysplasia, connective-tissue disorders, migraine, recent infection

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painful partial Horner syndrome**: ptosis + miosis, often without facial anhidrosis
Carotid: monocular visual loss, aphasia, contralateral weakness; pulsatile tinnitus possible
Vertebral: occipital pain, diplopia, ataxia, dysarthria, vertigo with central neurologic signs
Pain may precede ischemia by hours or days; normal initial neurologic examination does not exclude dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear or vasa vasorum hemorrhage → intramural hematoma and arterial narrowing
Mural thrombus embolization usually causes stroke; expansion may compress adjacent sympathetic fibers

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CTA head and neck** rapidly evaluates carotid/vertebral lumen and associated occlusion
MRA with fat-suppressed neck MRI identifies mural hematoma; brain MRI detects infarction
Tapered stenosis, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm support diagnosis; catheter angiography for equivocal/interventional cases
Do not rely on carotid ultrasound alone for distal carotid or vertebral lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Eligible acute ischemic stroke → **IV thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy**; dissection alone is no exclusion
★ Extracranial dissection → **antiplatelet or anticoagulation for 3–6 months**, individualized bleeding/ischemic risk
Repeat vascular imaging guides follow-up; no proven universal superiority of anticoagulation
Recurrent ischemia despite medical treatment or critical hemodynamic compromise → specialist consideration of stenting
Intracranial extension/subarachnoid hemorrhage → urgent neurovascular consultation; avoid reflex anticoagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: TIA, retinal infarction, ischemic stroke, dissecting pseudoaneurysm
Intracranial dissections may rupture into subarachnoid space; recurrent extracranial events uncommon

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid neck manipulation/contact injury while healing; control vascular risks
High-risk connective-tissue disease → individualized long-term activity counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cluster headache: episodic autonomic headache without persistent ischemic findings
Pancoast tumor: gradual Horner syndrome with shoulder/arm symptoms
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without focal deficits or acute neck pain

cervical-radiculopathy.name: Cervical radiculopathy
cervical-radiculopathy.scope: C5-C8 radiculopathy, cervical disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, LMN arm and UMN leg signs, Spurling test, conservative management, MRI cervical spine, surgical decompression
cervical-radiculopathy.core: Neck pain radiating down one arm with a dermatomal sensory deficit and reduced corresponding reflex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Disc herniation in younger adults; osteophytes and foraminal narrowing with aging
Repetitive neck loading, smoking, prior cervical injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Spurling test**: extension, ipsilateral rotation, axial compression reproduce arm symptoms
Shoulder abduction may relieve root pain
★ **Myelopathy**: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, LMN arms plus UMN legs; late bladder dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Root compression → segmental weakness; central canal stenosis → spinal cord dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: Map strength, sensation, reflexes; examine gait, plantar responses, Hoffmann sign
★ **Cervical MRI**: myelopathy, progressive deficit, cancer/infection concern, or failed conservative care
EMG/nerve conduction studies if localization uncertain; sensory responses usually preserved in radiculopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **NSAIDs + physical therapy**, activity modification; most improve within weeks
Persistent disabling root pain → consider epidural steroid injection or surgical referral
Cord compression or progressive motor deficit → urgent spine evaluation for decompression
Avoid cervical manipulation with suspected myelopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent denervation and muscle atrophy; untreated cord compression → irreversible disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ergonomic adjustments, neck strengthening, smoking cessation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carpal tunnel: median hand symptoms, positive Phalen, no neck provocation
Rotator cuff disease: painful shoulder motion, preserved distal neurologic examination
Brachial plexopathy: multiple roots/nerves, abnormal sensory nerve responses

child-abuse-and-neglect.name: Child abuse and neglect
child-abuse-and-neglect.scope: Physical abuse (burn patterns, fractures of different ages, metaphyseal corner fractures), abusive head trauma (shaken baby, subdural hematoma, retinal hemorrhages), neglect, mandatory reporting
child-abuse-and-neglect.core: Reasonable suspicion of child maltreatment requires protective reporting; proof and caregiver permission are unnecessary.

rows.label: Principle
items: Inconsistent history, delayed care, or developmentally impossible mechanism increase suspicion

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Report to child protective services** promptly; urgent danger → emergency protective services
Stabilize; document verbatim statements, findings and photographs; interview caregivers separately
★ Suspected physical abuse age <2 → **skeletal survey**; repeat after approximately 2 weeks

rows.label: Don't
items: Confront or accuse caregivers; promise secrecy; delay reporting for complete diagnostic certainty
Discharge into an unsafe setting; substitute reporting to a supervisor for mandated reporting

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Financial hardship alone ≠ neglect; assess ability to obtain food, shelter and medical care
Consider bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta and accidental trauma without delaying protection

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Metaphyseal corner/posterior rib fractures**; mixed healing stages → abuse concern
Immersion burns: uniform depth, sharp edges, stocking/glove pattern; nonmobile infants: sentinel bruising
★ Abusive head trauma: **subdural hemorrhage, extensive retinal hemorrhages**, unexplained encephalopathy

table.title: Presentation → evaluation
rows: AST/ALT, lipase, urinalysis; CT if concerning
Growth, nutrition, hygiene, supervision, unmet care needs

child-abuse-and-neglect.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric safeguarding principles; reporting procedures vary by jurisdiction.

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease
Anticholinergics, sedatives, alcohol, hearing loss, sleep apnea may worsen cognition

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving
Personality, language, executive, visuospatial, memory, motor symptoms help establish phenotype
Abrupt change, fluctuating attention, fever, focal deficits → evaluate acute superimposed illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alzheimer: amyloid plaques/tau tangles; Lewy/Parkinson: alpha-synuclein; vascular disease: ischemic neuronal injury
Frontotemporal degeneration affects frontal/anterior temporal networks, often before typical late-life onset

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**
Early biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer: specialist-selected antiamyloid drugs; baseline/serial MRI for ARIA

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity
Exercise, hearing correction, social engagement, vascular risk reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Delirium: hours–days, impaired attention, fluctuating awareness
Depression: prominent distress, variable effort, potentially reversible cognitive deficits
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-first decline, incontinence, ventriculomegaly; tap test may predict shunt response

table.title: Phenotype clues
rows: Insidious episodic-memory decline, later multidomain deficits
Stroke-related or stepwise decline, focal findings
Early hallucinations, fluctuation, REM behavior, parkinsonism
Early disinhibition/apathy or progressive aphasia; memory spared
Established motor disease >1 year before dementia

dementia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [Alzheimer's Association diagnostic guidance 2024](https://www.alz.org/news/2024/clinical-practice-guideline-evaluation-alzheimers), [NICE dementia](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations/); established subtype teaching.

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; depression may present as somatic complaints

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, stress responses, and neuroplasticity
Antidepressant benefit develops over weeks despite early changes in neurotransmitter availability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
PHQ-9 quantifies severity; interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger → **continuous observation and psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal psychotherapy; moderate/severe: SSRI such as sertraline + psychotherapy
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid eating disorders; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation, useful with anorexia/insomnia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after starting/changing drugs, family support with consent
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; depressive cognitive impairment often prominent complaints and variable effort
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

encephalitis.name: Encephalitis
encephalitis.scope: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), temporal lobe lesions, CSF analysis (elevated RBCs, lymphocytic pleocytosis, PCR), IV acyclovir, West Nile virus, autoimmune encephalitis
encephalitis.core: Fever with sustained altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits suggests brain inflammation and warrants immediate empiric acyclovir.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HSV-1 often occurs without immunosuppression; mosquito exposure suggests arboviruses
Autoimmune disease or tumor association; anti-NMDA receptor disease sometimes accompanies ovarian teratoma

rows.label: Clues
items: HSV: personality change, aphasia, olfactory hallucinations, focal seizures
★ **Temporal lobe abnormalities** strongly suggest HSV; hemorrhagic CSF possible but not required
West Nile: movement disorder or asymmetric flaccid weakness; anti-NMDA: psychosis, dyskinesia, autonomic instability
Reduced consciousness, status epilepticus, or respiratory compromise → ICU-level care

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV causes necrotizing inflammation, often limbic/temporal; mosquito-borne viruses infect neuronal tissue
Autoantibodies against neuronal surface antigens disrupt synaptic signaling

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **LP: CSF cells, protein, glucose, HSV PCR**; lymphocytes, ↑protein, usually normal glucose
Neuroimaging before LP for focal deficits, papilledema, marked impaired consciousness, or suspected mass effect
MRI more sensitive than CT; EEG identifies nonconvulsive seizures or temporal periodic discharges
Early negative PCR with strong suspicion → continue treatment and repeat CSF PCR in 3–7 days
West Nile: CSF IgM; autoimmune suspicion → CSF/serum antibodies and tumor search

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected HSV → **IV acyclovir immediately**, usually 14–21 days; do not await PCR
Airway/seizure support; possible bacterial infection → ceftriaxone + vancomycin; Listeria risk → add ampicillin
Acyclovir: renal adjustment, IV hydration; West Nile: supportive care
★ Autoimmune disease → **steroids, IVIG/plasma exchange**, tumor removal after infectious evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, focal deficits, death; acyclovir crystal nephropathy
Severe autoimmune disease: arrhythmia, hypoventilation, prolonged rehabilitation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mosquito repellent, protective clothing, vector control; no routine HSV encephalitis vaccine

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bacterial meningitis: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose; overlap requires empiric coverage
Toxic/metabolic delirium: systemic explanation without inflammatory CSF
Primary psychosis: lacks new seizures, dysautonomia, or focal neurologic abnormalities

encephalitis.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious and autoimmune neurology teaching.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence plus generalized tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration; levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

hearing-loss.name: Hearing loss
hearing-loss.scope: Conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss, Weber and Rinne tests, presbycusis, ototoxicity (cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics), noise-induced, Meniere disease, acoustic neuroma
hearing-loss.core: Distinguish impaired sound conduction from cochlear/nerve dysfunction; sudden sensorineural loss requires urgent treatment rather than observation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Aging, occupational/recreational noise, cerumen, chronic middle-ear disease
★ Ototoxins: **cisplatin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics**; risk increases with renal impairment and combined exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency loss, difficulty understanding speech amid background noise
Noise injury: high-frequency audiometric notch; tinnitus common
Ménière: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus, aural fullness
★ **Unilateral progressive loss + poor speech discrimination** → vestibular schwannoma; imbalance may accompany

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conductive: external/middle-ear transmission impaired; sensorineural: cochlea or auditory nerve damaged
Chronic noise/aging preferentially damages basal cochlear hair cells; Ménière involves endolymphatic hydrops

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy → tuning forks → formal audiometry**, including air/bone thresholds and speech testing
Tympanometry evaluates middle-ear mechanics; asymmetric sensorineural loss → MRI internal auditory canals
Sudden loss: ≥30 dB across ≥3 contiguous frequencies within 72 hours; urgent audiogram/ENT
Do not attribute sudden unilateral deficit to cerumen without confirming resolution after removal

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove cerumen, treat effusion/infection or structural cause; persistent conductive disease → ENT
★ Sudden sensorineural loss → **corticosteroids promptly**, within 2 weeks; intratympanic route possible
Chronic bilateral deficit → hearing aids, communication strategies; severe refractory loss → cochlear implant evaluation
Ménière: sodium moderation, selected diuretic; short-term vestibular suppressant during attacks
Vestibular schwannoma: observation, stereotactic radiation, or surgery according to tumor size and symptoms

rows.label: Complications
items: Communication barriers, social isolation, depression, impaired safety awareness
Ototoxicity can be permanent; vestibular injury can cause imbalance and falls

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hearing protection, safe listening levels, baseline/serial audiometry with ototoxic drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Auditory processing/cognitive disorder: difficulty understanding despite relatively preserved peripheral thresholds
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without hearing loss

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection: fever, rash, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy after recent exposure
Weight loss, oral thrush, recurrent infections suggest advanced immunodeficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB testing; pregnancy assessment
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin or TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary brain lesion, fails empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; induced sputum/BAL

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine or labetalol**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

intracranial-hemorrhage.name: Intracranial hemorrhage
intracranial-hemorrhage.scope: Intracerebral hemorrhage, hypertensive hemorrhage, amyloid angiopathy, coagulopathy reversal, blood pressure management
intracranial-hemorrhage.core: Acute focal neurologic deficits with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness require immediate CT to identify intraparenchymal bleeding and guide reversal.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Chronic hypertension, older age, anticoagulants/coagulopathy, stimulant use
Vascular malformation, tumor, venous thrombosis; lobar recurrence in older adults suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid progression, seizure, severe BP elevation; small bleeds may resemble ischemic stroke
★ Hypertensive sites: **putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum**; amyloid favors superficial lobar locations
Declining consciousness, asymmetric pupils, abnormal posturing → mass effect/herniation
Cerebellar injury: vomiting, severe ataxia, vertigo; rapid deterioration possible despite initially preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-artery lipohyalinosis or amyloid deposition weakens vessel walls
Expanding hematoma, intraventricular extension, and perihematomal edema cause secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT now**; CBC/platelets, INR/PTT, renal function, glucose, medication history
CTA/vascular imaging for younger patients, atypical location, suspected malformation; repeat CT for deterioration/expansion
MRI susceptibility imaging identifies microbleeds and underlying lesions after stabilization
Do not give thrombolysis or perform LP for established parenchymal hemorrhage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway, head elevation, neuro-ICU; **stop anticoagulants and reverse immediately**
★ Mild/moderate ICH, SBP 150–220 → IV **nicardipine/clevidipine**, target ~140, maintain 130–150 mm Hg
Large/severe ICH requires individualized perfusion goals; avoid abrupt excessive BP reduction or SBP <130
Cerebellar deterioration, hydrocephalus, brainstem compression, or volume ≥15 mL → **urgent surgical evacuation**
Hydrocephalus → ventricular drain; herniation → hypertonic saline/mannitol; treat seizures, no routine prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, herniation, seizures, disability, recurrent hemorrhage
★ **No routine platelet transfusion** for antiplatelet-associated ICH without emergency surgery/severe thrombocytopenia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Long-term BP control, smoking/stimulant cessation; reassess anticoagulation using recurrence and embolic risks
Intermittent pneumatic compression immediately; low-dose heparin prophylaxis after bleeding stability is documented

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic stroke: no acute blood on CT; SAH: thunderclap, sulcal/cisternal blood
Hemorrhagic tumor: mass/edema pattern, enhancement; confirm with MRI

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness localizes to the ipsilateral carotid circulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: Aphasia or neglect suggests cortical involvement; crossed cranial-nerve/limb findings suggest brainstem disease
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF → oral anticoagulation with timing based on infarct/bleeding risk; high-intensity statin, BP control
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lysosomal-storage-diseases.name: Lysosomal storage diseases
lysosomal-storage-diseases.scope: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A, cherry-red spot), Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase, hepatosplenomegaly), Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase), Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase), Fabry disease
lysosomal-storage-diseases.core: Progressive neurologic regression, organ enlargement, skeletal disease, or childhood neuropathic pain can reflect failure of lysosomal substrate degradation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Most autosomal recessive; Fabry X-linked, with symptomatic females possible
Family history/consanguinity; ancestry modifies some carrier risks but disease occurs across populations

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Infantile **regression** or loss of milestones requires metabolic/genetic evaluation
Cherry-red macula reflects storage in surrounding retinal ganglion cells; not unique to one disorder
Angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal verticillata with episodic burning extremity pain favor Fabry

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Absent lysosomal enzyme → intracellular substrate accumulation and progressive cell dysfunction
CNS injury may become irreversible before systemic disease is obvious

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Targeted enzyme assay + molecular testing** guided by phenotype; newborn screening varies by region
Fabry in females: molecular testing essential because enzyme activity can be normal
CBC, liver/spleen imaging, cardiac/renal assessment according to suspected disease; biopsy usually unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Gaucher systemic disease → **imiglucerase** or other enzyme replacement; substrate reduction for selected adults
Fabry → **agalsidase beta**; selected amenable variants → migalastat; manage proteinuria, pain and cardiac disease
Presymptomatic/very early Krabbe → urgent transplant-center assessment; established neurologic damage poorly reversible
Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency → specialist olipudase alfa for non-CNS manifestations
Tay-Sachs: supportive care, seizure control, nutrition and airway support; no established curative treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, seizures and early death in severe infantile neurodegenerative forms
Gaucher: fractures/osteonecrosis, cytopenias; Fabry: CKD, cardiomyopathy, early stroke

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Carrier/cascade testing and reproductive counseling**; early detection permits treatment before irreversible damage
Monitor affected families' renal, cardiac and neurologic function

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mitochondrial disease: maternal pattern, lactic acidosis, nonvascular stroke-like episodes
Glycogen storage disease: fasting hypoglycemia or exercise phenotype rather than broad lysosomal signs

lysosomal-storage-diseases.evidence: ASMD treatment checked 2026-10-30: [FDA Xenpozyme](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-trials-snapshots/drug-trials-snapshots-xenpozyme); established biochemical phenotypes.

macrocytic-anemia.name: Macrocytic anemia
macrocytic-anemia.scope: Folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
macrocytic-anemia.core: MCV >100 fL prompts separation of megaloblastic DNA-synthesis failure from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and marrow disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vegan diet without supplementation, gastric bypass, ileal disease/resection, metformin → B12 depletion
Alcohol misuse, poor intake, pregnancy, methotrexate, trimethoprim → folate depletion
Autoimmune gastritis → pernicious anemia; nitrous oxide functionally inactivates cobalamin

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis; ineffective erythropoiesis may raise LDH/indirect bilirubin and lower other cell lines
★ **Paresthesias, gait ataxia, impaired vibration/proprioception** → B12 deficiency, even without anemia
Smooth macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils indicate megaloblastic change

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective thymidine synthesis delays nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasm
B12-dependent myelin metabolism explains spinal cord/peripheral nerve injury; folate deficiency lacks this syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, smear, reticulocytes, B12**; assess folate, liver tests, TSH, exposures
Borderline B12 → methylmalonic acid; renal impairment can elevate it independently
★ Suspected pernicious anemia → **anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies**; highly specific but not fully sensitive
High reticulocytes → bleeding/hemolysis; unexplained cytopenias/dysplasia → bone marrow evaluation for MDS
Coexisting iron deficiency may normalize MCV; neurologic suspicion still requires B12 evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Replace B12 before or with folate**; folate alone can conceal ongoing neurologic injury
Neurologic/severe deficiency or malabsorption → parenteral B12 initially; irreversible cause requires lifelong replacement
Dietary B12 deficiency may respond to high-dose oral replacement; folate deficiency → oral folic acid
Remove causative drug/exposure where possible; monitor reticulocyte response and count recovery

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated B12 deficiency → irreversible neurologic disability; severe disease → pancytopenia
Pernicious anemia → increased gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumor risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reliable B12 supplementation for vegans**; lifelong monitoring/replacement after relevant GI surgery
Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy; improve nutrition and reduce harmful alcohol intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol-associated macrocytosis: round macrocytes, no required megaloblastic change
Myelodysplasia: persistent multilineage cytopenia, dysplastic marrow
Reticulocytosis: polychromasia after blood loss or hemolysis

macrocytic-anemia.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology and nutritional teaching.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; CSF leak → pneumococcus; advanced HIV/transplant → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
